options.a: Outreach training on recognizing workplace hazards
options.b: A required license to work in general industry
options.c: An OSHA compliance inspection of the employer's site
options.d: Training that certifies a worker as a competent person

distractorExplanations.b: OSHA 10 is voluntary outreach training that ends with a completion card; it is not a license or a federal work permit.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses outreach training with enforcement: inspections are run by OSHA compliance officers, not trainers.
distractorExplanations.d: An OSHA 10 card does not make anyone a competent person; the employer designates one based on capability plus authority to correct hazards.

options.a: Refuse any assigned task they dislike and still be paid for the shift
options.b: Report hazards to OSHA only after first getting their supervisor's approval
options.c: A safe workplace and to raise hazard concerns without illegal retaliation
options.d: Choose which OSHA standards apply to their own job and skip the others

distractorExplanations.a: The right to refuse is narrow: imminent danger, good-faith belief, no time for an inspection, and the employer was asked to fix it, not dislike.
distractorExplanations.b: Workers may file a complaint with OSHA directly and confidentially; no supervisor approval is required before contacting OSHA.
distractorExplanations.d: Employers must comply with every applicable standard; workers cannot opt out of standards that cover their tasks.

options.a: Provide a workplace free from every hazard, whether recognized or not
options.b: Pay for everyday safety-toe boots that workers wear off the job
options.c: Post the OSHA 300 log year-round in a visible location
options.d: Provide a workplace free from recognized serious hazards

distractorExplanations.a: The General Duty Clause covers recognized hazards causing or likely to cause death or serious harm, not every conceivable hazard.
distractorExplanations.b: 1910.132(h) exempts non-specialty safety-toe footwear worn off the jobsite from the employer-paid PPE rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the 300 log with the Form 300A summary, which is posted from February 1 to April 30, not year-round.

options.a: Reported and used to prevent future incidents
options.b: Recorded on the OSHA 300 log as a first-aid case
options.c: Reported only if a supervisor witnessed the event
options.d: Treated as closed once nobody was hurt by it

distractorExplanations.b: A near miss with no injury is not recordable, and first-aid cases are excluded from the 300 log as well.
distractorExplanations.c: Anyone who sees a near miss should report it; requiring a supervisor witness suppresses a key leading indicator.
distractorExplanations.d: The lack of injury was luck; a near miss exposes the same hazard that can injure someone next time, so it needs follow-up.

options.a: Rank workers by how often they report injuries
options.b: Replace the need for engineering controls with PPE
options.c: Document injuries after they happen for the 300 log
options.d: Break tasks into steps and control hazards

distractorExplanations.a: A JHA analyzes the steps of a task, not individual workers; ranking people by reports discourages injury reporting.
distractorExplanations.b: A JHA selects controls using the hierarchy; it does not justify swapping engineering controls for PPE.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the proactive job hazard analysis with reactive injury recordkeeping on OSHA Form 300.

options.a: Pause unsafe work under employer programs/rights frameworks
options.b: Pause unsafe work only after OSHA has inspected the site
options.c: Leave the job permanently with full pay if they see a hazard
options.d: Override lockout tags placed by other workers to finish a task

distractorExplanations.b: Stop-work authority is used immediately when a hazard is seen; waiting for an OSHA inspection defeats its purpose.
distractorExplanations.c: Stop-work pauses the task until the hazard is controlled; it is not a right to quit with continued pay.
distractorExplanations.d: Stop-work halts work; it does not let anyone remove another worker's lockout device, which only the person who applied it may remove.

options.a: Identify the worker at fault and issue discipline
options.b: Find root causes and prevent recurrence
options.c: Wait until the insurance claim has been settled
options.d: Focus on the injury's cost rather than its causes

distractorExplanations.a: Blame-focused investigations stop at the immediate act and discourage reporting; root-cause analysis looks at system failures.
distractorExplanations.c: Investigations should start promptly while evidence and witness memories are fresh, not after a claim closes.
distractorExplanations.d: Cost tracking does not prevent recurrence; the investigation must find the causes so controls can be fixed.

options.a: Hazards are reported early and fixed
options.b: Crews win prizes for zero reported injuries
options.c: Only injuries that need a doctor get reported
options.d: Hazards are logged but fixed at the annual audit

distractorExplanations.b: Incentives tied to zero reported injuries discourage reporting, and OSHA warns they can amount to retaliation.
distractorExplanations.c: Minor injuries and near misses are leading indicators; reporting only medical cases hides hazards until someone is badly hurt.
distractorExplanations.d: Delaying correction to an annual audit leaves workers exposed and teaches them that reporting changes nothing.

options.a: PPE first, because it protects each worker directly
options.b: Administrative controls before engineering controls
options.c: Elimination or substitution before relying on PPE alone
options.d: Warning signs and training before machine guarding

distractorExplanations.a: PPE is the least effective tier of the hierarchy because it depends on correct fit, use, and maintenance by each worker.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses two tiers: engineering controls rank above administrative controls such as procedures and scheduling.
distractorExplanations.d: Signs and training are administrative controls, which rank below engineering controls like machine guards.

options.a: Replacing the formal training that OSHA standards require
options.b: Recording injuries for the annual OSHA 300A summary
options.c: Short, focused hazard communication on the job
options.d: Long annual classroom reviews of every standard

distractorExplanations.a: Toolbox talks supplement but do not replace standard-specific training such as HazCom or lockout/tagout instruction.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses brief safety meetings with recordkeeping; the 300A summary is a records form, not a training method.
distractorExplanations.d: Toolbox talks are brief, frequent, on-site, and topic-specific, the opposite of a long annual classroom session.

options.a: Any worker who has completed an OSHA 10-hour outreach training course
options.b: A person holding an engineering degree or certificate who designs the systems
options.c: An OSHA compliance officer who inspects the site and issues citations
options.d: Someone capable of identifying hazards and authorized to take corrective action

distractorExplanations.a: An OSHA 10 card alone does not create a competent person; it takes hazard recognition plus employer-given authority to correct.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes OSHA's qualified person (degree, certificate, or professional standing), not the competent person with corrective authority.
distractorExplanations.c: The competent person is designated by the employer on site; OSHA compliance officers enforce rules and are not that role.

options.a: Recording every first-aid case on the OSHA 300 log
options.b: Posting the 300A summary from January through December
options.c: Keeping injury logs for one year before discarding them
options.d: Tracking work-related injuries and illnesses as required

distractorExplanations.a: First-aid-only cases (bandages, nonprescription-strength medication) are not recordable on the 300 log.
distractorExplanations.b: The Form 300A summary is posted from February 1 to April 30, not for the whole calendar year.
distractorExplanations.c: Forms 300, 300A, and 301 must be kept for five years following the year they cover, not one year.

options.a: Each employer protecting only its own workers from its own hazards
options.b: Coordination so hazards created by one party do not harm others
options.c: The host employer taking sole responsibility for every crew's safety
options.d: Separate safety rules for each trade with no shared site meetings

distractorExplanations.a: Under OSHA's multi-employer policy, creating, exposing, correcting, and controlling employers can all be cited for hazards to others.
distractorExplanations.c: Each employer keeps duties to its own workers; a controlling employer owes reasonable care, not sole responsibility.
distractorExplanations.d: Isolated trade rules without coordination let one crew's hazards (openings, overhead work) injure another crew.

options.a: Delivered in English for every worker on the site
options.b: Completed once at hire and then not repeated
options.c: Understood by workers for the hazards they face
options.d: Documented with a signature even if not understood

distractorExplanations.a: OSHA requires training in a language and vocabulary that each worker understands, not English by default.
distractorExplanations.b: Retraining is needed when tasks, hazards, or equipment change, and some standards require periodic refreshers.
distractorExplanations.d: A signed roster does not show comprehension; OSHA looks at whether workers actually understood the training.

options.a: Slips, trips, and falls
options.b: Noise-induced hearing loss
options.c: Ladder rung failures
options.d: Hand-arm vibration

distractorExplanations.b: Noise is controlled with engineering controls and hearing conservation; tidy floors do not change sound levels.
distractorExplanations.c: Rung defects are caught by inspecting the ladder before use; floor housekeeping does not prevent ladder failure.
distractorExplanations.d: Vibration exposure is managed by tool selection and limiting exposure time, not by keeping walkways clear.

options.a: Marked and cleaned promptly
options.b: Marked and left to air-dry
options.c: Covered with flattened cardboard
options.d: Cleaned at the end of the shift

distractorExplanations.b: A warning sign alone leaves the slip hazard in place; the spill still needs prompt cleanup, not air-drying.
distractorExplanations.c: Cardboard soaks through, becomes slick, and can slide underfoot, creating a new slip and trip hazard.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting until the end of the shift leaves the wet floor exposed to traffic for hours; clean it promptly.

options.a: Are acceptable as permanent wiring
options.b: Are safe once taped to the floor
options.c: Need only a GFCI to remove the risk
options.d: Create trip hazards if misused

distractorExplanations.a: Flexible cords may not substitute for fixed wiring under 1910.305(g); extension cords are temporary only.
distractorExplanations.b: Tape loosens and traffic damages the cord; reroute it or use a proper cord cover rather than relying on tape.
distractorExplanations.c: A GFCI protects against shock but does nothing about the trip hazard a cord creates across a walkway.

options.a: The tallest ladder available
options.b: Any ladder with all rungs intact
options.c: Lightest weight for easy carrying
options.d: Height, duty rating, and task

distractorExplanations.a: An oversized ladder is harder to set at the correct 4:1 angle; the ladder length must match the working height.
distractorExplanations.b: Intact rungs are an inspection criterion, not a selection criterion; height and duty rating still have to fit the job.
distractorExplanations.c: Carrying convenience ignores the duty rating (Type IA, I, II, III) needed for the user's weight plus tools and materials.

options.a: Two hands and one foot, or two feet and one hand, in contact while climbing
options.b: One hand, one foot, and the body leaning on the ladder while climbing
options.c: Both feet and a hand-held tool braced against the ladder while climbing
options.d: Ladder tied off at the top, footed at the base, and set at a 4:1 angle

distractorExplanations.b: Leaning the body against the ladder is not a point of contact; three limbs must be on the ladder at all times.
distractorExplanations.c: A tool braced on the ladder is not a grip; hands should be free, with tools carried on a belt or hoisted.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses ladder setup (securing and the 4:1 angle) with the three-point climbing technique the question asks about.

options.a: Proper erection, access, and fall protection
options.b: Inspection only after the scaffold is fully loaded
options.c: Climbing the cross braces to reach the platform
options.d: Erection by any crew member who has climbed one before

distractorExplanations.b: A competent person inspects scaffolds before each shift and after any event that could affect integrity, not after loading.
distractorExplanations.c: Cross braces may not be used as a means of access; ladders, stair towers, or ramps are required.
distractorExplanations.d: Scaffolds must be erected by trained workers under the supervision of a competent person, not anyone with experience climbing.

osha-10-general-readiness-check-walking-.explanation: Proper erection, access, and fall protection as applicable. Fall protection is required as the scaffold standard applies to the platform height and scaffold type.

options.a: Heat stress in indoor work areas
options.b: Noise-induced hearing loss
options.c: Falls and struck-by incidents
options.d: Hand-arm vibration injuries

distractorExplanations.a: Heat stress depends on temperature, humidity, and workload; dim lighting does not drive heat illness.
distractorExplanations.b: Hearing loss comes from noise exposure; lighting levels have no effect on decibel levels.
distractorExplanations.d: Vibration injuries come from tool exposure time and tool design, not from how well an area is lit.

options.a: Handrails only where a stairway has ten or more risers
options.b: Riser heights that vary to fit the available space
options.c: Painted treads with a gloss finish for easy cleaning
options.d: Adequate lighting and compliant handrails where required

distractorExplanations.a: Handrails or stair rails are required at four or more risers or more than 30 inches of rise, not ten risers.
distractorExplanations.b: Stairs need uniform riser heights and tread depths; uneven risers are a classic trip hazard.
distractorExplanations.c: Gloss paint lowers traction; stair treads need slip-resistant surfaces, not easy-clean glossy coatings.

options.a: Faster movement to limit time exposed
options.b: Slower movement and hazard scanning
options.c: Relying on ankle-high boots instead of scanning
options.d: Walking backward to watch the crew

distractorExplanations.a: Speed on uneven ground increases trips and falls; shortening exposure time does not offset the higher fall risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Good footwear helps, but it does not replace slowing down and watching for holes and debris.
distractorExplanations.d: Walking backward hides the ground ahead, which is exactly where the holes and uneven spots are.

options.a: Be placed in designated, marked storage areas
options.b: Block exits or create fall/trip exposures
options.c: Be stacked with heavier items on lower levels
options.d: Use cross-tied, interlocked stacks for stability

distractorExplanations.a: Staging in designated, marked areas is good practice, so it is not something staging should avoid.
distractorExplanations.c: Placing heavier items low is the recommended stacking practice for stability, not a prohibited one.
distractorExplanations.d: Cross-tying or interlocking layers is a recommended way to stabilize stacks, so it should not be avoided.

options.a: Casters are locked before anyone climbs up
options.b: The base width is extended with outriggers
options.c: Height stays within the base-width ratio limit
options.d: Overreaching or moving occupied equipment unsafely

distractorExplanations.a: Locking casters before climbing reduces rolling and tipping; it lowers risk rather than raising it.
distractorExplanations.b: Outriggers widen the base and increase stability, which reduces the chance of tipping.
distractorExplanations.c: Staying within the height-to-base ratio (such as 4:1 for mobile scaffolds) keeps the unit stable.

options.a: Salting walkways once at the start of the week
options.b: Piling plowed snow against exit doors to clear lots
options.c: Rubber-soled boots alone without clearing paths
options.d: Removal, traction, and footwear policies

distractorExplanations.a: Ice and snow conditions change daily; salt and traction material must be reapplied as conditions change.
distractorExplanations.b: Piling snow at exits blocks emergency egress and creates melt-and-refreeze ice at the doors.
distractorExplanations.c: Traction footwear is one layer; paths still need snow and ice removal and treatment.

options.a: Toeboards, canopies, hard hats, and exclusion zones
options.b: Bump caps in place of Type I hard hats under loads
options.c: Stacking tools along open platform edges for reach
options.d: Warning signs below work areas, with no barricades

distractorExplanations.b: Bump caps are not ANSI Z89.1 rated for falling objects; they only protect against minor bumps.
distractorExplanations.c: Tools along an unguarded edge are a prime falling-object source; toeboards and setbacks prevent this.
distractorExplanations.d: Signs alone are an administrative control; an exclusion zone needs barricades that keep people out.

osha-10-general-readiness-check-walking-.explanation: Toeboards, canopies, hard hats, and exclusion zones as needed. Use these controls as needed for the overhead work and the people below.

options.a: Learn the brand names of the products they use
options.b: Know which chemicals OSHA has banned from use
options.c: Read SDSs only when an exposure has happened
options.d: Know chemical hazards and protective measures

distractorExplanations.a: HazCom is about hazards and protective measures; knowing brand names says nothing about how a chemical can hurt you.
distractorExplanations.b: HazCom is a right-to-know rule about hazards, not a list of banned chemicals.
distractorExplanations.c: SDSs must be readily accessible and workers trained before exposure, not consulted only after an incident.

options.a: Pricing, supplier discounts, and reorder details
options.b: Workplace injury rates for the chemical's users
options.c: Hazards, first aid, handling, and PPE information
options.d: OSHA citation history for the product's maker

distractorExplanations.a: The 16-section SDS gives supplier identity and contact, not pricing or ordering information.
distractorExplanations.b: Injury rates come from OSHA 300 records and BLS data, not from a chemical's safety data sheet.
distractorExplanations.d: An SDS covers the product's hazards and handling; enforcement history for the manufacturer is not part of it.

options.a: Be replaced by the SDS once it is filed in the area
options.b: Remain legible and convey required hazard information
options.c: Show only the product name the worker recognizes
options.d: Be removed once a container is half empty

distractorExplanations.a: An SDS on file does not replace the container label; both are required under HazCom.
distractorExplanations.c: Workplace labels need the product identifier and hazard information, not just a familiar product name.
distractorExplanations.d: Labels must stay on as long as the container holds the chemical, whatever the remaining volume.

options.a: No label if refilled from a labeled drum
options.b: Identification and hazard warnings
options.c: Only the supplier's original barcode
options.d: The DOT shipping placard number

distractorExplanations.a: The exemption covers only portable containers for immediate use by the worker who filled them, not any refilled container.
distractorExplanations.c: A barcode identifies stock, not hazards; workplace labels need the product identifier and hazard warnings.
distractorExplanations.d: DOT placards and numbers are for transport; workplace containers need HazCom hazard labeling.

osha-10-general-readiness-check-hazcom-0.explanation: Identification and hazard warnings per HazCom rules. HazCom requires the product identifier and hazard warnings unless the portable-container immediate-use exemption applies.

options.a: Storage in open pans for ventilation and bonding when the weather is dry
options.b: Grounding the receiving can only, with ignition sources kept within reach
options.c: Proper storage, grounding/bonding where required, and ignition control
options.d: Storage near heat for viscosity, with fire extinguishers as the main control

distractorExplanations.a: Open containers release flammable vapors, and bonding is needed during every transfer, not only in dry weather.
distractorExplanations.b: Both containers must be bonded with the dispensing one grounded, and ignition sources must be kept away.
distractorExplanations.d: Heat raises vapor generation, and extinguishers respond after ignition instead of preventing it.

options.a: Harm only through long-term inhalation
options.b: Cause harm once heated above room temperature
options.c: Be neutralized by rinsing with vinegar
options.d: Burn skin and eyes on contact

distractorExplanations.a: Corrosives cause immediate tissue damage on contact; they are not limited to chronic inhalation effects.
distractorExplanations.b: Corrosives burn skin and eyes at normal temperatures; heating is not needed for them to injure.
distractorExplanations.c: First aid is flushing with large amounts of water; neutralizing on skin can add a heat-producing reaction.

options.a: Dust masks for organic solvent vapors
options.b: Respirators without a fit test or medical evaluation
options.c: Holding breath during short exposures
options.d: Ventilation and respirators per the program

distractorExplanations.a: Filtering facepieces stop particles, not organic vapors; vapors require the proper cartridge respirator or ventilation.
distractorExplanations.b: 1910.134 requires a medical evaluation and fit test before a tight-fitting respirator is used.
distractorExplanations.c: Holding breath is not a control; even brief exposures can exceed limits, so ventilation or respirators are needed.

options.a: Diluted with water and mopped into a floor drain
options.b: Handled by trained people with proper materials
options.c: Cleaned up by whoever is nearest to the spill
options.d: Covered with paper towels until the next shift

distractorExplanations.a: Dilution can spread the chemical and send it to drains, causing environmental release; use proper absorbents.
distractorExplanations.c: Untrained responders risk exposure; spills are handled by trained people using the SDS and spill kit.
distractorExplanations.d: Paper towels do not contain or neutralize most chemicals, and leaving a spill for the next shift prolongs exposure.

options.a: Stored together if containers are tightly capped
options.b: Kept separate — no chemical storage with lunches
options.c: Kept on separate shelves in the same refrigerator
options.d: Stored together when the chemical is non-toxic

distractorExplanations.a: Capped containers can still leak or contaminate surfaces; food must not be stored where toxic materials are.
distractorExplanations.c: Separate shelves in one refrigerator still allow contamination; food and chemicals need separate storage units.
distractorExplanations.d: Even low-hazard chemicals can contaminate food, and the sanitation rule bars food storage where toxic materials are present.

options.a: Hazard classes at a glance
options.b: The supplier's company identity
options.c: Required PPE for each task
options.d: DOT shipping class numbers

distractorExplanations.b: Supplier identity is a separate label element; pictograms show the hazard class, not who made the product.
distractorExplanations.c: PPE appears in precautionary statements; GHS pictograms communicate hazard classes such as flammable or corrosive.
distractorExplanations.d: DOT labels and placards are for transport classes; GHS pictograms on workplace labels show hazard classes.

options.a: Within 30 days of the first use
options.b: At the next annual refresher
options.c: Before workers are exposed
options.d: After the SDS has been revised

distractorExplanations.a: HazCom training happens at initial assignment and before exposure to a new hazard, not within 30 days after use.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting for the annual refresher leaves workers exposed to a new chemical without training.
distractorExplanations.d: Training is triggered by a new hazard entering the work area, not by the timing of an SDS revision.

options.a: Workers handle sealed, unopened containers
options.b: Only flammable liquids are dispensed
options.c: Corrosives or other splash hazards exist
options.d: Workers wear safety glasses at the task

distractorExplanations.a: Sealed containers with no opening or transfer present little splash potential, which is what triggers eyewash needs.
distractorExplanations.b: Eyewash and showers under 1910.151(c) are tied to injurious corrosive materials, not flammability alone.
distractorExplanations.d: Safety glasses do not remove the need for flushing facilities where corrosives can splash.

options.a: Use the container label alone until the audit
options.b: Use another brand's SDS for the same use
options.c: Request it within 30 days while using it
options.d: Obtain it before using the chemical blindly

distractorExplanations.a: The label is not a substitute for the SDS; the employer must have the SDS available before the chemical is used.
distractorExplanations.b: Formulations differ between products; another brand's SDS may list different hazards and first aid.
distractorExplanations.c: Using the chemical while waiting for the SDS means workers lack hazard and first-aid information during exposure.

options.a: The first control to use, before guarding
options.b: A last line of defense after other controls
options.c: A substitute for engineering controls
options.d: Equal in rank to administrative controls

distractorExplanations.a: PPE comes after elimination, substitution, engineering, and administrative controls, not before machine guarding.
distractorExplanations.c: PPE supplements engineering controls; it does not replace guards or ventilation that remove the hazard.
distractorExplanations.d: In the hierarchy, PPE ranks below administrative controls as the last line of defense.

options.a: Deduct the cost of required PPE from pay
options.b: Provide required PPE and training on use
options.c: Provide PPE but leave training to the vendor
options.d: Pay for everyday safety-toe boots worn off-site

distractorExplanations.a: Under 1910.132(h), employers pay for required PPE, with limited exceptions such as everyday safety-toe footwear.
distractorExplanations.c: 1910.132(f) makes the employer responsible for training each worker on when and how to use PPE.
distractorExplanations.d: Non-specialty safety-toe footwear that workers may wear off the job is an exception to employer payment.

options.a: Impact and penetration hazards to the head
options.b: Noise exposures above the 85 dBA action level
options.c: Arc flash burns to the face and neck
options.d: Falls from heights above four feet

distractorExplanations.b: Noise above the action level calls for hearing protection, not a hard hat.
distractorExplanations.c: Arc flash protection needs arc-rated face shields and clothing; a hard hat alone does not protect the face.
distractorExplanations.d: Falls are prevented by guardrails or fall arrest systems; hard hats protect against impact to the head.

options.a: Glasses with side shields seal better against splash
options.b: They give the same splash protection if rated Z87
options.c: Goggles are rated for impact but not for splash
options.d: Goggles generally seal better against splash

distractorExplanations.a: Side shields add impact protection from the side but do not seal; goggles are needed for splash.
distractorExplanations.b: The Z87 mark covers impact; splash protection requires goggles marked D3 for droplets and splash.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the point: goggles seal around the eyes and are the choice for chemical splash.

options.a: Noise exceeds 100 dBA for any length of time
options.b: A worker first reports ringing in the ears
options.c: Noise exceeds 90 dBA averaged over a full week
options.d: Noise exposures warrant it under the program

distractorExplanations.a: The trigger is the 85 dBA 8-hour TWA action level; 100 dBA is just one point on the exposure table.
distractorExplanations.b: Ringing is a symptom of damage already done; protection is based on measured exposure, before symptoms.
distractorExplanations.c: OSHA noise limits use an 8-hour time-weighted average, not a weekly average.

options.a: The chemical or cut hazard
options.b: The worker's preferred grip feel
options.c: One general-purpose cotton type
options.d: The thickest material on hand

distractorExplanations.b: Comfort matters, but glove material must be chosen for the specific chemical or cut hazard first.
distractorExplanations.c: Cotton absorbs chemicals and offers little cut resistance; no single glove fits every hazard.
distractorExplanations.d: Thickness is not chemical resistance; permeation depends on glove material matched to the chemical.

options.a: Fit testing once at hire, with no medical evaluation required
options.b: A shared respirator cleaned at the end of each week
options.c: Medical clearance, training, and fit testing when applicable
options.d: Training only, since N95 masks need no fit test

distractorExplanations.a: 1910.134 requires a medical evaluation before use and fit testing annually, not once at hire.
distractorExplanations.b: Shared respirators must be cleaned and disinfected before being worn by another person, not weekly.
distractorExplanations.d: Required N95 filtering facepieces are tight-fitting and do need fit testing under the respiratory program.

options.a: Anchored to any fixed pipe or conduit nearby
options.b: Inspected once a year by the manufacturer
options.c: Kept in service after arresting a fall
options.d: Inspected and used correctly for the task

distractorExplanations.a: Anchors must support 5,000 lb per worker or be engineered; pipes and conduit are not rated anchorages.
distractorExplanations.b: Users inspect fall protection before each use, with periodic competent-person checks, not a yearly factory check.
distractorExplanations.c: Equipment that has arrested a fall must be removed from service until a competent person clears it.

options.a: Replace barriers and flaggers between workers and traffic
options.b: Workers be seen by vehicle and equipment operators
options.c: Protect workers from cuts and abrasions
options.d: Workers stay cool under direct sunlight

distractorExplanations.a: High-visibility apparel adds conspicuity; it does not replace physical barriers or flaggers in work zones.
distractorExplanations.c: Hi-vis garments are about being seen; cut protection comes from gloves and cut-resistant sleeves.
distractorExplanations.d: Hi-vis colors are chosen for visibility, not cooling; heat stress needs water, rest, and shade.

options.a: Repaired with duct tape
options.b: Removed from service
options.c: Used until the shift ends
options.d: Cleaned and reissued

distractorExplanations.a: Improvised repairs do not restore the rated protection; damaged PPE must be taken out of service.
distractorExplanations.c: Damaged PPE may fail during the shift; it must be removed from service as soon as damage is found.
distractorExplanations.d: Cleaning does not fix cracks, tears, or worn parts; damaged PPE is removed from service, not reissued.

options.a: Slips on wet or oily floors
options.b: Ankle sprains on uneven ground
options.c: Compression and impact to toes
options.d: Chemical splashes on the shin

distractorExplanations.a: Slip resistance comes from the outsole tread and compound, not from the steel toe cap.
distractorExplanations.b: Ankle support depends on boot height and fit; a steel toe protects the toes, not the ankle.
distractorExplanations.d: Shin splash protection needs chemical-resistant boots or covers; the steel toe protects against impact and compression.

options.a: Hard hats for overhead impact
options.b: Safety glasses for impact/splash
options.c: Respirators for vapor exposure
options.d: Hearing protection for noise

distractorExplanations.a: Face shields protect the face, not the head; overhead impact protection comes from the hard hat.
distractorExplanations.c: A face shield does not filter air; vapor exposure is handled by ventilation or respirators.
distractorExplanations.d: A face shield does nothing for noise; hearing protection is a separate piece of PPE.

osha-10-general-readiness-check-ppe-elec.explanation: Safety glasses for impact/splash — they may not replace primary eye protection alone. Face shields are secondary protection worn over safety glasses or goggles; they may not replace primary eye protection alone.

options.a: Workers handle flammable liquids
options.b: Voltage is below 50 volts
options.c: Work is done on de-energized gear
options.d: Electrical arc hazards exist

distractorExplanations.a: Flammable liquid handling calls for ignition control and flame-resistant clothing for flash fire, not arc-rated gear.
distractorExplanations.b: Below 50 volts, NFPA 70E generally does not require arc flash protection; arc-rated gear applies where arc hazards exist.
distractorExplanations.c: Equipment verified de-energized under lockout/tagout has no arc hazard, so arc-rated clothing is not the trigger.

options.a: Weekly
options.b: Once a year
options.c: Before use
options.d: Monthly

distractorExplanations.a: Damage can occur any day; PPE is inspected before each use, not on a weekly schedule.
distractorExplanations.b: An annual check misses daily wear and damage; PPE must be inspected before each use.
distractorExplanations.d: A monthly check leaves weeks of use with possibly damaged PPE; inspect it before each use.
